newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine reappoints bank head, economists thrilled.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine reappoints bank head, economists thrilled.

text.p: Ukraine's parliament awarded champion reformer Viktor Yushchenko a second term as central bank chief on Wednesday, soothing economists who had been horrified at the thought conservatives might block his appointment.
"Yushchenko is firmly in the saddle, so everybody's breathing huge sighs of relief. He's so important to Ukraine's economy," said one Western economist who asked not to be named.
Yushchenko's tight monetary policies are loved by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and reformers who credit him with cutting inflation and nurturing stable financial policies.
Inflation skydived to 39.7 percent last year from 10,000 percent when Yushchenko was appointed in 1993 -- a year which brought massive miners' strikes and near economic collapse.
Under Yushchenko, the bank has won more independence and issued the hryvnia currency, which has fallen to 1.87 per dollar from 1.76 when it was introduced in September 1996.
Economists were especially cheered by the fact that Yushchenko won a comfortable majority and that speaker Olexander Moroz, head of the conservative Socialist Party, backed him.
"Up to now he was supported only by the commercial banks and by the president, but not by parliament and government," said Marcin Luczynski of George Soros' advisory group.
Once the well-dressed Yushchenko -- accused by conservatives of looking "too much like a movie star" and being an IMF puppet -- only had support from President Leonid Kuchma and bankers.
But Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko, a pragmatist who has some support from conservatives, and now parliament gave him a solid mandate and that was a healthy sign, economists said.
Communists, who contributed to 87 votes against Yushchenko compared to 257 for, were furious because Moroz refused to give them a chance to speak on Wednesday.

They blame monetary reforms for a pension and wage arrears mountain put at 3.9 billion hryvnias ($2.1 billion) which brought hundreds of miners to parliament's doorstep on Tuesday to demand their pay.
Kuchma has promised to solve this back-payments problem by mid-year but monetary reforms also face some opposition from industrialists who want more credits to the economy.

Gross domestic product fell by 10 percent last year while industrial output fell 5.2 percent, but Yushchenko said the industrialists should wait as the economy would soon deliver credit for investment.
"We need patience. In the second quarter we can move from the policy of stable currency to the policy of long-term credits to the Ukrainian economy," he told the chamber.
He said $1 billion would be distributed in the form of short-, medium- and long-term credits this year, without specifying where the money would come from.

Ukraine, whose foreign investment has been put at $1.5 billion since it won independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, is hoping for a new $2.5-$3 billion credit deal from the IMF which is holding talks in Kiev this week.

Reformist deputy Sergei Teryokhin saw a long-term role for Yushchenko with parliamentary elections scheduled for March 1998 and presidential polls in October 1999. "Then the person running the financial policy can become key," he told reporters.
Another economist said Yushchenko's great strength was that he was a tough reformer as well as a smooth political operator.
"It's not like all economic reforms depend on one person. It's just that it would be a leap into the unknown if he wasn't reappointed," he said.
